questions.question: Give a short note on division of labour at home.
questions.solution_html:
• Examine how stereo types reinforce inequality.
  •  Rigid Role Expectations: Men are seen as breadwinners, women as homemakers,
  • limiting opportunities.
  •  Education Barriers: Girls are often discouraged from pursuing science or
  • leadership roles.
  •  Workplace Discrimination: Women face the “glass ceiling” and wage gaps due to
  • biased assumptions.
  •  Media Representation: Stereotypical portrayals of women as dependent and
  • emotional reinforce inferiority.
  •  Cultural Practices: Traditions like dowry and son preference reflect deep-rooted
  • gender bias.
  •  Political Underrepresentation: Leadership is often viewed as a male domain.
  •  Economic Dependence: Gender roles limit women’s access to property and credit.
  •  Violence Justification: Stereotypes sometimes normalize control or abuse against
  • women.
  •  Internalization: Both men and women internalize stereotypes, reproducing them
  • unconsciously.
  •  Breaking the Cycle: Education, awareness, and gender-sensitive media can
  • challenge these stereotypes
  • [CO1]

questions.question: Give an example of gender sensitivity in daily life. [2x5 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• Demonstrate how CEDAW promotes equal rights for women in education.
  •  Article 10 Commitment: Ensures equal access to education at all levels for girls
  • and women.
  •  Non-Discrimination Clause: Prohibits exclusion from schools based on gender or
  • marital status.
  •  Curriculum Equality: Promotes elimination of gender bias in textbooks and
  • teaching methods.
  •  Vocational and Technical Training: Encourages women’s participation in non-
  • traditional fields.
  •  Scholarships and Support: Urges states to provide financial aid to increase
  • women’s access.
  •  Dropout Prevention: Recommends measures to reduce female dropout rates,
  • especially due to early marriage.
  •  Teacher Training: Supports gender-sensitivity training for educators.
  •  Adult Education: Encourages literacy and lifelong learning opportunities for
  • women.
  •  Monitoring by States: Requires periodic reporting on educational progress for
  • women.
  •  Impact in India: Influenced policies like Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Beti Bachao Beti
  • Padhao, and gender-inclusive curricula.
  • [CO4]

questions.question: Explain how gender budgeting promotes gender equity in India.
questions.solution_html:
• Critically discuss gender identity and orientation.
  •  Gender Identity: Refers to an individual’s personal sense of being male, female,
  • both, or neither.
  •  Biological vs. Social: While sex is biological, gender identity is shaped by
  • psychological and social factors.
  •  Orientation Defined: Sexual orientation refers to the pattern of emotional,
  • romantic, or sexual attraction (e.g., heterosexual, homosexual, bisexual, asexual).
  •  Cultural Influence: Society defines acceptable gender roles, influencing identity
  • expression.
  •  Transgender and Non-binary Identities: Challenge binary notions of gender and
  • demand recognition.
  •  Discrimination: People with diverse gender identities often face stigma, violence,
  • and exclusion.
  •  Legal Protection: India’s Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019
  • upholds the right to self-identify one’s gender.
  • [CO1]

questions.question: Compare the objectives of GEI and GII.
questions.solution_html:
• Compare the objectives of GEI and GII.
  • Aspect Gender Empowerment Index(GEI) Gender Inequality Index (GII)
  • Objective Measures women’s participation in political and economic life. Measures gender-based disadvantage across health, empowerment, and labour.
  • Focus Areas Political representation, income, and professional opportunities. Maternal health, adolescent birth rates,education, and representation.
  • Goal Highlight women’s empowermentand participation. Highlight inequality between men and women.
  • Interpretati
  • Higher value = more
  • empowerment. Higher value = more inequality.
  • Use Guides empowerment policies. Identifies gender disparities needing intervention.
  • [CO1]

questions.question: Express the value of equal pay policies in closing the gender gap.
questions.solution_html:
• Express the value of equal pay policies in closing the gender gap. /
  •  Definition: Equal pay policies ensure men and women receive the same
  • remuneration for the same or equivalent work.
  •  Economic Justice: Promotes fairness and acknowledges women’s contribution to
  • the workforce.
  •  Empowerment: Increases women’s economic independence and decision-making
  • power.
  •  Reduced Discrimination: Discourages biased hiring and occupational
  • segregation.
  •  Example: Equal Remuneration Act (1976) in India promotes wage parity,
  • supporting Sustainable Development Goal 5 on gender equality.
  • [CO6]

questions.question: Explain femininity as a cultural construct.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain femininity as a cultural construct.
  •  Definition: Femininity refers to traits, roles, and behaviors culturally associated
  • with being female.
  •  Cultural Basis: Defined by social norms and expectations rather than biology.
  •  Variation: Varies across societies and time—what is considered “feminine” in one
  • culture may differ in another.
  •  Impact: Shapes gender roles, beauty standards, and career choices.
  •  Example: Caring, emotional expression, and modesty are often promoted as
  • “feminine” traits through socialization.
  • [CO1]
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss how sex influences social identity.
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss how sex influences social identity.
  •  Definition: Sex refers to biological differences (male, female, intersex), while social
  • identity is shaped by social roles and expectations.
  •  Role Assignment: Societies assign different responsibilities and privileges based
  • on sex.
  •  Socialization: From birth, individuals are taught behaviors aligning with their sex
  • (e.g., girls nurtured for caregiving roles).
  •  Inequality: Creates hierarchies and stereotypes that can limit opportunities.
  •  Relevance: Recognizing this helps promote equality and challenge rigid gender
  • norms.
  • [CO2]

questions.question: Describe reforms in medieval India addressing gender.
questions.solution_html:
• Describe reforms in medieval India addressing gender.
  •  Bhakti Movement: Saints like Mirabai and Akka Mahadevi challenged caste and
  • gender barriers through spiritual expression.
  •  Social Reformers: Basavanna and Kabir promoted equality and condemned gender
  • discrimination.
  •  Religious Equality: Women saints gained recognition as spiritual leaders, breaking
  • patriarchal norms.
  •  Education: Some reformers supported women’s access to learning through
  • religious teachings.
  •  Impact: Though limited, these movements sowed early seeds for women’s dignity
  • and equality.
  • [CO2] 1

questions.question: Discuss role of missionaries in women’s education. [5x4 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss role of missionaries in women’s education.
  •  Early Efforts: Christian missionaries in the 19th century established schools for
  • girls in India.
  •  Curriculum: Focused on literacy, moral education, and later vocational and teacher
  • training.
  •  Key Contributors: Organizations like the Serampore Mission and Madras Mission
  • pioneered girls’ schools.
  •  Social Impact: Empowered women to enter professions like teaching and nursing.
  •  • Legacy: Helped challenge orthodox restrictions and laid the foundation for
  • women’s educational advancement in India.
  • [CO1]
